prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B015 for Katori and Ye. After reading the full exchange, the scientific case rests on three points that no member disputes. The result is real and independently reproduced, with Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks reaching 10^-18-class performance in several laboratories. It has a unique figure of merit, a fractional uncertainty that can be checked. And the credit divides cleanly into Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, which cancels the lattice light shift while keeping many atoms in parallel, and Ye's realisation of record systematic uncertainty and stability. The chair's first question asked which element is not covered by the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. My answer is the many-atom, light-shift-free interrogation that separates the lattice clock from the single-ion clock. The comb supplied the ruler and ion control supplied the quantum-limited reference, but neither delivered the statistical advantage that moved stability by orders of magnitude. The downstream uses (tests of relativity and varying constants, dark-matter searches, geodesy, the redefinition of the second) are already being exercised. I would not hold the award for the formal redefinition, since that is a metrological decision about units and does not alter the physics of the discovery.
statement.case_against: I take the competing case more seriously after round 1 than I did at the opening. B017 is the broader discovery: a sharp prediction (2011) followed by experimental observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states (2018) opened a new regime of quantum matter, and five members rank it in their top three. If the committee decides that a new regime of physics outranks a measurement invention, B017 should come first, and I would not call that a mistake. B015 still carries overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and two names leave other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST and JILA colleagues, RIKEN) outside the citation. I have not verified the detailed priority sequence among them. These are real costs. My judgment is that they are smaller than the cost of B017's credit boundary, in which Yuan Cao and the other experimental groups and the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists sit outside three names, and in which the Bistritzer name is contested.

responses.point: Danielsson argued that the pairing mechanism is not a Nobel test for B017, and that if I rank pulsar-timing evidence (B004) third I should not apply a stricter maturity test to B017.
responses.response: The consistency charge is fair and I accept most of it. The test is whether the discovery is secure, not whether it is fully interpreted, and the correlated and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene are reproduced in many laboratories. I therefore withdraw maturity as a reason to rank B017 below B015. The pulsar-timing evidence is also a weaker case on that same test, which is why B004 is not in my preferred configuration and I do not propose it. What remains between us is credit. Three names must cover a prediction by MacDonald and Bistritzer and an experimental discovery that was a group effort, with Cao and others omitted. I do not think a citation can repair that, and the Nobel Committee's three-person limit makes it harder here than for the two-name clock.

responses.point: Kroll agreed on B015 but warned that the two of us are experimentalists who like instruments with a number attached, and that B017 has broader top-three support while the pairing mechanism should not delay it.
responses.response: The warning is well taken, and I treat my own opening rank of B017 as the lowest of any member, eighth, as something to discount for field bias, not to defend. I agree with Kroll that the open mechanism is not a reason to defer, and I now side with him against my own round-1 phrasing on that. Where I still differ from a pure breadth-of-support argument is that top-three counts say the committee finds B017 important, not that the credit is settled. His own reservation, that the experimental credit sits with a group, is the one that decides it for me. If the committee resolves the credit question to its satisfaction, B017 moves ahead of B015 on my ballot, and I record that openly.

responses.point: Eriksson would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero for B017, which treats Bistritzer as joint with MacDonald, and he prefers B051 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp).
responses.response: A two-name B017 would improve the credit question for me, because it answers the charge of padding the theory side. But it would also formalise the exclusion of Bistritzer, whose 2011 paper with MacDonald is the specific prediction of the magic angle, and it would leave Cao outside as before. That trade does not make B017 cleaner than B015, which needs no cut. On B051 my view is unchanged from round 1. The conceptual change is secure, but the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, the 2D versus 3D split with Hasan, and the 2016 topological-phases prize leave a contested boundary around the third seat that the clock does not have.

responses.point: Olsson agreed on the credit for B015, said B017 might be preferred if experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero were clarified, and objected to combining a clock prize with a single-name IceCube part.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The two clock names use most of the three places, so I do not propose a second part, and I withdraw the IceCube idea as a companion since a single-name large-collaboration credit is not a fair configuration. On her conditional, that B017 would be preferred if the experimental credit is clarified, I think the committee has to be honest that the credit may not be clarifiable. The first-author and the group question are historical facts, not matters for further study, so I would not hold the clock prize for that.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; my answer is yes but it is a judgment, not a measurement.
Whether other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST/JILA colleagues, RIKEN) have a priority claim that undermines a two-person configuration; I have not independently verified the priority record.

Whether B017 should come ahead of B015 if the committee prefers a new regime of physics to a precision-measurement invention, and whether its credit boundary around Cao, Bistritzer and the other groups can be defended in three names.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second; I think not, but I accept that it could be read either way.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B015, B017 or B016. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle physics) concern cosmic-ray and gamma-ray instrumentation and do not overlap with optical clocks, moire materials or cold-atom work. As chair I note that I prefer B015, and I have tried to state the B017 and B051 positions on their own terms. I also note that I share an experimental background with Kroll-Stefan and Olsson-Eva that may bias us toward instrument-driven results. No recusal is required of me, and I see no recusal needed from the disclosures in the chair summary beyond what the committee decides for the people who raised them.
